messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Alessandro had always been drawn to the sea, and as a fisherman, he spent most of his days on the water. But it was on land, in a damp and dingy cell, that his life took a drastic turn. He was captured by a group of armed men while traveling abroad, and what followed was a blur of pain, fear, and disorientation. Alessandro remembered the sound of his own screams, the feeling of his body contorting into unnatural positions, and the sensation of his skin burning from cuts and bruises. The memories lingered long after he escaped, and even now, two years later, they still haunted him. The sound of babies crying on a bus ride home from work was enough to transport him back to that cell. He would feel his body stiffen, his muscles tensing as if preparing for another round of torture. His mind would flash with images of the event, and he would feel an overwhelming rage wash over him. He tried to avoid public transportation whenever possible, opting instead to drive or walk long distances rather than risk being triggered by the sound of children's wails. Alessandro also struggled with feelings of vulnerability. When he felt emotionally exposed, even in the safety of his own home, he would become hyper-vigilant, constantly scanning his surroundings for potential threats. He noticed things that others might overlook - a sharp object on the kitchen counter, a suspicious noise outside - and his mind would start to weave worst-case scenarios. His back had to be against a wall wherever he went, so he could see what was coming at him from every angle. It made social gatherings difficult, but Alessandro felt like he had no choice. The more he thought about the event, the more memories flooded his mind. He would remember the sound of footsteps outside his cell door, signaling another round of interrogation. He would recall the pain in his shoulders and back as he was forced to hold a particular position for hours on end. His body would even reenact those positions when memories came flooding back - Alessandro's wife had woken up one night to find him curled into a fetal ball, his muscles taut with tension. As these memories resurfaced, so did the threat response. Alessandro began to feel like he was walking on eggshells all the time, waiting for the next shoe to drop. He became withdrawn and isolated, avoiding friends and family in an attempt to shield himself from the world outside his home. The irony was not lost on him - by trying to avoid triggers, he had inadvertently created a prison of his own making. One evening, as Alessandro was driving home from work, he noticed a group of rowdy teenagers loitering near the bus stop. His heart began racing, and his mind started spinning scenarios about potential threats lurking in every corner. He pulled over to collect himself before realizing that this cycle of fear was no longer tenable. The isolation was affecting his marriage, his friendships, and even his livelihood as a fisherman - something had to give. With the support of his wife, Alessandro finally made an appointment with a therapist, hoping to break free from the tangled web of memories and fears that had been holding him hostage for so long. As he sat in the waiting room, fidgeting nervously, Alessandro couldn't shake off the feeling that he was taking the first tentative steps into unknown waters - but at least this time, he wasn't alone.
